deep.reconstruction:
The page has two unrelated items.

(A) 'Cubaturcoefficienten' (cubature coefficients). There are four triangular arrays, each with its total written above it. Each entry is the weight at a point of the regular grid of a triangle: barycentric coordinates (i/n, j/n, k/n), n = 1..4. Dividing a weight by the total gives the coefficient of f at that node in a rule approximating the mean value of f over the triangle.
- n=1, total 3: weights 1,1,1 at the vertices. Mean = (f1+f2+f3)/3, exact for degree 1.
- n=2, total 3: weight 0 at the vertices and 1 at the edge midpoints. Mean = (sum of the three midpoint values)/3, exact for degree 2.
- n=3, total 120:
  - vertices 4 (1/30);
  - the six edge points at 1/3 and 2/3 get 9 (3/40);
  - the centroid gets 54 (9/20).
  - Check: 3*4 + 6*9 + 54 = 120.
- n=4, total 45:
  - vertices 0;
  - the six edge points next to a vertex (3/4,1/4,0) get 4;
  - the three edge midpoints get -1;
  - the three interior points (1/2,1/4,1/4) get 8.
  - Check: 0 + 24 - 3 + 24 = 45.

These are the closed Newton–Cotes formulas for the triangle of orders 1–4. My check, using mean(l1^a l2^b l3^c) = 2 a! b! c!/(a+b+c+2)!:
- the 120-rule reproduces l1^3 (1/10), l1^2 l2 (1/30) and l1 l2 l3 (1/60);
- the 45-rule reproduces l1^4 (1/15) and l1^2 l2^2 (1/90).
So the rules are exact to degrees 1, 2, 3, 4 respectively.

(B) 'Vertheilung der absolut kleinsten Reste complexer Primzahlen in zwei Classen'. Take a Gaussian prime pi = A + Bi of norm p ≡ 1 (mod 4), with A odd and B even. The absolutely least residues mod pi are the p-1 nonzero lattice points z with z/pi in the open square |Re|, |Im| < 1/2. They are split into:
- Class I: divisible by 1+i, i.e. x+y even.
- Class II: not divisible by 1+i.
Multiplication by i preserves both the square and the parity of x+y, so Gauss tabulates one quarter, (p-1)/4 residues. The columns are p, (A,B), #I, #II, #I - #II. Two of my checks:
- p=13, pi = 3+2i: the 12 residues are ±1, ±i (odd), ±1±i (even), ±2, ±2i (even). The quarter gives 2, 1, +1, as tabulated.
- In every row #I + #II = (p-1)/4, and #I is always even.

Rule I (Gauss). Take the modulus ≡ 1 (mod 2+2i), i.e. A+B ≡ 1 (mod 4). Here AX + BY = p/2 is the edge Re(z/pi) = 1/2 of the residue square, i.e. the line 2BY = A^2 + B^2 - 2AX.
- Take all integers X with A/2 - B/2 < X < A/2. There are B/2 of them.
- For each, put eps = (-1)^(X + floor(Y)).
- Then sum(eps) = #I - #II.
- Example p=97, (9,4): 8Y = 97 - 18X.
  - X=4: 8Y=25, floor(Y)=3, eps=-1.
  - X=3: 8Y=43, floor(Y)=5, eps=+1.
  - Sum = 0, as tabulated.

Alternative rule (continued overleaf). Take the integers Y with B/2 < Y < B/2 + A/2, i.e. (A-1)/2 of them. Get X from 2AX = A^2 + B^2 - 2BY and sum (-1)^(floor(X) + Y). For A+B ≡ 3 (mod 4) the next page says the first rule still holds and the second needs a correction of -1.

My verification of rule I against every row of the table:
- I recomputed rule I for p = 5, 13, 17, 29, 37, 41, 53, 61, 73, 89, 97, 101, 109, 113, 137, 149, 157, 173, 181, 193, 197, 241, 257, 269, 277.
- I used the given (A,B) and allowed negative X. This covers the rows with A+B ≡ 3, e.g. 5: (1,2); 61: (5,6), sum -3; 181: (9,10), sum -5; 113: (7,8), sum -4.
- Every value agrees with the last column.
- The blank rows come out as: 229 (15,2) -> -1, i.e. 28/29; 233 (13,8) -> +2, i.e. 30/28.

Geometrically (my interpretation), the count works column by column. Along each lattice column, the alternating parity sum of a segment depends only on its endpoints. Only the endpoints on the edge Re(z/pi) = 1/2 survive; the rest cancel by the symmetry of the square.

Purpose. This is evidently connected with Gauss's biquadratic-residue work: the role of 1+i, and Gauss-lemma-type counting with residues in the square. I could not match sum(eps) directly to the known quartic character i^((a-b-b^2-1)/4) of 1+i, so the exact intended application is unsure.
errors: No arithmetic errors found. All 25 filled rows of the residue table agree with Gauss's Rule I as I recomputed it.
The rows for 229 and 233 are left blank. By the rule they should read 28, 29, -1 and 30, 28, +2.

As stated on this page, the condition 'modulus ≡ 1 mod (2+2i)' is too restrictive. Many tabulated primes (5, 29, 37, 61, 73, 101, 113, 137, 173, 181, 193, 197, 241, 269, 277) have A+B ≡ 3 (mod 4), i.e. are ≡ 3 mod (2+2i). The next page addresses this, noting the first rule still holds for these.
Neither counting rule is proved on the page. They are stated and checked by example only.

results.what: Weights for 3-, 6-, 10- and 15-point cubature on a triangle at the regular barycentric grid: (1,1,1)/3; midpoints only; vertices 4, edge 9, centroid 54 over 120; vertices 0, near-vertex edge 4, midpoints -1, interior 8 over 45. These are exact to degrees 1–4.
results.modern_name: Closed Newton–Cotes (equally spaced Lagrange-node) cubature formulas for the triangle
results.usually_credited_to: Tabulated systematically in 20th-century numerical analysis (e.g. Hammer–Marlowe–Stroud 1956, Silvester 1970). Low-order cases appear in finite-element literature.

results.what: Table of the split of the (p-1)/4 quarter of absolutely least residues mod a Gaussian prime A+Bi into those divisible and not divisible by 1+i, for all p ≡ 1 mod 4 up to 277
results.modern_name: Parity count of lattice points in the fundamental square of Z[i]/(pi); Gaussian-integer analogue of Gauss's lemma data
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum 1828/1832 and Nachlass); Eisenstein for Gauss-lemma proofs of quartic laws

results.what: Rule: sum over integers X in (A/2 - B/2, A/2) of (-1)^(X + floor((A^2+B^2-2AX)/(2B))) equals #ClassI - #ClassII; alternative sum over Y
results.modern_name: Lattice-point (Eisenstein/Zeller-type) counting formula along an edge of the residue square
results.usually_credited_to: Lattice-point counting of this kind is usually associated with Eisenstein (1844) for reciprocity proofs

deep.surprise_reason: The residue-class table and the floor-function counting rule fit Gauss's known (partly published, partly Nachlass) biquadratic-residue investigations. They are a notable unpublished computational detail rather than a new theorem. The closed Newton–Cotes triangle cubature weights (the 120 and 45 rules) are a modest surprise as an early appearance of formulas usually found in 20th-century tables, though such weights are elementary to derive.
